blocks.text: **The problem.** `citations[i]` is how many times a researcher's i-th paper has been cited. Their **h-index** is the largest `h` such that they have **at least h papers with at least h citations** each. Return it.

blocks.alt: Citations 3, 0, 6, 1, 5 sorted from most to least cited: 6, 5, 3, 1, 0, drawn as bars. A diagonal marks rank 1, 2, 3 and so on. The first three bars reach at least their rank — 6 at least 1, 5 at least 2, 3 at least 3 — but the fourth, 1, is below 4. So the h-index is 3.

elements.text: sort most cited first; h = how many bars reach their rank

blocks.text: The idea: sorted, the h-th best paper decides

Sort the citations from most to least cited. Then "h papers with at least h citations" means: the first h papers all have at least h — and since they're sorted, only the **weakest of them**, the h-th, needs checking. So walk down the sorted list while paper number `h + 1` still has at least `h + 1` citations. Where that fails, h is the answer.
**Time O(n²), space O(1).** Up to n candidate values of h, each counted over all n papers.

blocks.caption: Sorted most cited first, h grows while paper #(h+1) still has at least h+1 citations.

blocks.code:
def h_index(citations):
    c = sorted(citations, reverse=True)   # most cited first
    h = 0
    while h < len(c) and c[h] >= h + 1:   # the (h+1)-th best paper has at least h+1 citations
        h += 1
    return h

blocks.text: **Time O(n log n), space O(n)** for the sorted copy.

h can never exceed n, so any paper with more than n citations can be counted as n. Count how many papers have each number of citations from 0 to n, then walk down from n adding up papers until the total reaches the current value.
**Time O(n), space O(n).** A counting sort in disguise — the key insight is capping at n.

blocks.alt: Try every h: O(n²) time, O(1) space. Sort, then count: O(n log n) time, O(n) space. Counting: O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: **Every paper cited a lot** — h = n; it can't exceed the number of papers.
**Off by one** — paper number h + 1 (index h) is the one checked against h + 1.
**H-Index II** — the citations are already sorted ascending: binary search for the boundary in O(log n) (see the Searching course).
**Kth Largest Element** — another question about how values rank once sorted (Arrays and Heap courses).
**Maximum Gap** — counting and buckets again, used to beat O(n log n). Later in this course.
